claims.text: A like-for-like ranking on shared figures is not valid: each firm discloses its client-asset and net-new-asset metrics on a different basis (and its advisor-headcount metric differently), so no shared, same-basis measure of wealth-transfer capture exists. On the qualitative evidence, Schwab appears most prepared: it is the only firm that discloses an explicit wealth-transfer retention rate (about 75% of assets retained in a wealth transfer event) and frames its retail business as 'built to win across generations,' alongside about 70% of new-to-firm retail households being Gen Z and Millennial and 80% of retail assets held by U/HNW households, with the CEO stating its retention rate around wealth transfers is extremely high. By contrast, Edward Jones attributes declining net new assets in part to generational wealth transfers outside the firm, while Morgan Stanley, Merrill, and Raymond James show preparedness mainly through advisor succession, next-generation advisor development, and family-office/estate/trust capabilities rather than a stated transfer-retention figure.
